message.reasoning_content:
Locale is en_US.UTF-8, giving different collation. The task asks 字典序（区分大小写）which most naturally means byte/ASCII case-sensitive order → LC_ALL=C gives Apple, apple, fig, pear, plum. Both are "dictionary order" but case-sensitive requirement implies distinguishing case → C locale is the safest deterministic interpretation.

Hmm, but in en_US.UTF-8, case IS still distinguished (both apple and Apple present, so it distinguishes case — it doesn't dedupe them together). The difference is only ordering of Apple vs apple. "区分大小写" means case-sensitive (don't merge Apple and apple). Both satisfy that. But which ordering? To make it deterministic and standard for a "sort" task, use LC_ALL=C byte order. I'll go with LC_ALL=C.

Let me write the final files deterministically.

function.name: shell
function.arguments:
{"command": "set -e
mkdir -p out
# 1) sum of all integers
awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) s+=$i} END{printf "%d\n", s}' data/a.txt > out/sum.txt
# 2) unique words, case-sensitive ASCII (C locale) lexicographic order
tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' < data/b.txt | grep -v '^$' | LC_ALL=C sort -u > out/words.txt
# 3) notes
SUM=$(cat out/sum.txt); CNT=$(wc -l < out/words.txt)
printf 'sum of integers in data/a.txt = %s; unique words in data/b.txt = %s (sorted case-sensitively: %s)\n' "$SUM" "$CNT" "$(paste -sd, out/words.txt)" > out/notes.txt
echo "=== out/sum.txt ==="; cat out/sum.txt
echo "=== out/words.txt ==="; cat out/words.txt
echo "=== out/notes.txt ==="; cat out/notes.txt
echo "=== verify sum ==="; awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) s+=$i} END{print s}' data/a.txt
echo "=== verify unique count ==="; tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' < data/b.txt | grep -v '^$' | LC_ALL=C sort -u | wc -l"}
